The letter from the bank in Malmö was addressed to Ulla, but Henrik opened it by mistake while sorting the post at the kitchen counter. A repayment reminder. A loan he had never heard of, taken out eleven months ago, for more than they had saved in five years.

He read it twice. Then he looked around the flat as if it belonged to someone else: the new kettle, the calendar with her brother Jonas's birthday circled in red.

When Ulla came in with the shopping, he held up the page. "Is this real?"

She set the bags down very slowly. "Jonas's workshop was going under. I was going to tell you."

Henrik laughed once, without any humour. He thought of every evening he had sat with her going over their budget, nodding. What else had she been nodding through?

qa.q: What did Henrik open by mistake while sorting the post?
qa.a: He opened a letter from the bank addressed to Ulla, a repayment reminder for a loan he had never heard of.

qa.q: How can you tell Henrik feels made a fool of, not just surprised?
qa.a: He laughs once without humour and remembers all the evenings he sat going over their budget with her, nodding; he feels humiliated and shocked, and suddenly doubtful about what else she hid.

qa.q: What small step could help Henrik in the next hour, before the conversation turns into a fight?
qa.a: He could say plainly that he is too shocked to talk well right now and agree a time later that day to hear the whole story, instead of cross-examining her in the doorway.

qa.q: What might Ulla be feeling as she sets the bags down so slowly?
qa.a: She is probably frightened and ashamed, caught before she was ready, and torn between loyalty to Jonas and knowing she has hurt Henrik.

grounding: Henrik learns that his wife Ulla hid a large loan taken for her brother and is left shocked, humiliated and doubting what else he has missed.

The loan officer at the bank branch in Aizawl turned her screen so Farhan could see it. "Sir, before we process the home loan, there is an existing personal loan in your wife's name. The repayments come from your joint account."

Farhan stared at the number. Lalremsiami sat beside him, filling in the address section, and her pen stopped.

"There must be a mistake," he said, and heard how thin his voice was.

He turned to her. "What is this?"

She did not look up. "It was for my brother Mapuia's college fees. Last year. I meant to—"

The officer found a sudden interest in her stapler. Farhan felt heat climb up his neck. Two strangers in the queue behind them had heard. He had been the one explaining to the officer how careful they both were with money. Now he sat there wondering which other papers in their cupboard he had never read.

qa.q: Where do Farhan and Lalremsiami find out about the loan?
qa.a: At the bank branch in Aizawl, when the loan officer checks before processing their home loan.

qa.q: What is Farhan feeling when heat climbs up his neck?
qa.a: He feels humiliated and shocked, because he had just told the officer how careful they both were, and strangers in the queue heard.

qa.q: What could Farhan do right there at the desk to avoid making things worse?
qa.a: He could ask the officer to pause the application and say to Lalremsiami that they will talk about it at home today, so the first real talk is not in front of strangers.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami experience this moment?
qa.a: She is likely mortified that it came out in public and afraid of Farhan's reaction, while still believing she helped Mapuia for a good reason.

grounding: The passage shows a husband's shock and sense of being made a fool when a bank officer reveals his wife's hidden loan for her brother's college fees, and his sudden doubt about other papers.

Jahnavi,

I am writing this at two in the morning on the balcony because if I try to say it out loud I will shout, and I don't want Pinky to wake up to that.

I saw the SMS from the lender on your phone when you asked me to check the train timing. Four lakh. Taken in March. For Mahesh bhaiya's shop, I suppose, since he suddenly had new shutters in April.

I keep thinking of the Diwali dinner at your mother's, when Mahesh thanked "both of us" and I smiled like an idiot because I didn't know what he meant. Everyone at that table knew except me.

And now I'm lying awake going through every "it's nothing, just office" you said this year. I don't know which ones were true.

I'm not leaving. I just need you to tell me everything, all at once, tomorrow.

Your husband,
Jagdish

qa.a: At two in the morning on the balcony.

qa.q: Why does the Diwali dinner memory hurt Jagdish so much?

qa.q: Was writing a letter instead of talking straight away a good choice, and why?
qa.a: It was a sensible choice: he avoids shouting while Pinky sleeps, and he says clearly what he needs next, which is a full account tomorrow.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi feel when she reads that he is going through every "it's nothing, just office"?

grounding: Jagdish's letter shows a husband's shock, humiliation and new doubt about everything else after finding the loan his wife took for her brother.

They were already forty minutes late for his cousin's engagement, stuck in traffic on the ring road, when Ravish finally asked the question he had been holding since morning.

"Why didn't you just tell me, Shreya?"

She stared at the brake lights ahead. Her phone buzzed on her lap: her brother, again, probably to say thank you again.

"Because you would never have agreed," she said. "You'd have given me the lecture about how Nikhil always needs saving. I didn't have time for a lecture. He had a week."

Ravish's jaw went tight. "So it's my fault you lied."

"I didn't say that."

"You just did."

She turned her phone face down. Part of her wanted to say sorry. A louder part was still ten years younger, sitting at her parents' table, being told that a daughter's family comes second after marriage. The car crept forward. Nobody spoke until the venue.

qa.q: Who keeps calling Shreya during the drive?
qa.a: Her brother keeps calling, probably to say thank you again.

qa.q: What is Shreya feeling when she turns her phone face down?
qa.a: She feels torn and ashamed: part of her wants to apologise, but a louder part feels defensive, remembering being told a daughter's family comes second after marriage.

qa.q: What went wrong in how Shreya answered Ravish, and what could she say instead?
qa.a: Her reason blamed him for her secret, so he heard it as "it's your fault"; she could admit that hiding it was wrong first, and explain her fear of his judgement afterwards.

qa.q: How does Ravish hear "you would never have agreed"?
qa.a: He hears it as her blaming him for her lie, so his hurt grows and his jaw goes tight.

grounding: Shreya defends hiding a loan for her brother by saying her husband would never have agreed, which deepens his hurt while she stays torn between family loyalty and fear.

Salma washed the same glass three times while Tenzin sat at the dining table in their Pune flat with the bank statement.

She had rehearsed this. On the bus home she had lined up every reason: her brother's rent was three months behind, her father's pride, the landlord's threats. She had told herself she hid the loan to protect Tenzin from worry.

But when he said, very quietly, "Six months, Salma," the rehearsed speech fell apart and something sharper came out.

"You would never have agreed. You'd have looked at me the way you're looking at me now, like my family is a burden you married by mistake."

Tenzin put the statement down. "I have never said that."

"You didn't have to."

She turned back to the sink. Her hands were shaking. She knew she had just made it about him, and she could not seem to stop.

qa.q: How long had Salma kept the loan hidden, according to Tenzin?
qa.a: Six months.

qa.q: How can you tell Salma is ashamed even while she defends herself?
qa.a: Her hands shake, she keeps washing the same glass, and she knows she has just made it about Tenzin but cannot stop; under the defensiveness she feels ashamed and afraid.

qa.q: What could turn this conversation around at this stage?
qa.a: Salma could stop defending, say plainly that hiding the loan was wrong, and then tell Tenzin about her fear of being judged as a separate thing, not as a reason that blames him.

qa.q: What is it like for Tenzin to hear that she expected to be judged?
qa.a: He feels accused of something he never said, which adds a new hurt on top of the secret itself.

grounding: Salma, who hid a loan for her brother fearing judgement, defends herself with "you would never have agreed" and adds to her husband's hurt.

I noticed it first with the tea. Eshaan used to hand me my cup without looking up from his newspaper. Now he watches my face while I drink it, as if the answer to some question is written there.

This was a month after I told him about the loan I took for my brother. He said he forgave me. I think he meant it.

But he started checking the joint account every morning before brushing his teeth. When my phone rang, his eyes went to the screen before mine did. Once I laughed at a message from my cousin and he asked, too quickly, "Who's that?"

I am his wife, not a suspect. That's what I wanted to shout. But I also saw how grey he looked, how badly he was sleeping. He wasn't hunting me. He was bracing for the next blow.

Knowing that didn't stop it from hurting. I just felt watched in my own home.

— Harsha

Session note, 14 June

Uday and Kamini attended their third session. Uday arrived first and waited in the corridor checking his phone; when Kamini came in, his eyes went straight to her face and stayed there.

Uday described checking their accounts each night after she sleeps. He said, "If I stop, I feel I'm walking with my back to the door." He looked exhausted and mentioned losing sleep.

Kamini said she disclosed the loan to her brother in full two months ago and has hidden nothing since. "I am being punished for being honest," she said, and cried. Uday looked stricken at this.

I reflected back that his checking seems to be an attempt to prevent another shock, and that it is costing him rest and costing her the sense of being forgiven. Both agreed.

Next step: they will try a fixed weekly time to look at the accounts together, and we will review how it felt at the next session.

— Nilesh, counsellor

qa.a: He said it feels like walking with his back to the door.

qa.q: What was Kamini feeling when she said she was being punished for being honest?

qa.q: What does the counsellor's approach do well here?
qa.a: Nilesh names the checking as an attempt to prevent another shock rather than as an attack, so both can agree, and then offers a concrete next step, a weekly shared look at the accounts.

qa.q: Why might Uday look stricken when Kamini cries?
qa.a: He may suddenly see that his checking, meant to protect himself, is hurting her deeply, which likely leaves him guilty and torn.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows Uday's hypervigilant checking after his wife's hidden loan, how it exhausts him and makes Kamini feel watched rather than forgiven.

passage:
The power had gone out in the village, so Aparna lit the lantern and sat on the floor across from Govind before he could even take off his chappals.

"I'm going to tell you all of it, and you don't have to ask twice," she said. "Please let me finish."

She counted it on her fingers. The loan from the self-help group in January. The second one from the moneylender in Rampur when the first wasn't enough. How much her brother still owed. The gold earrings she had pawned and told him were at her mother's.

Govind's face changed at the earrings.

"That too," she said. "I hid it because I was ashamed, and hiding it was wrong. Not a mistake. Wrong."

She pushed a folded paper across the floor: every amount, every date she could remember. "I may have one date wrong. But there is nothing else. If you find something, it's because I forgot, not because I'm still hiding."

qa.q: What had Aparna told Govind about the gold earrings?
qa.a: She had told him they were at her mother's, when she had pawned them.

qa.q: Why does Aparna insist on calling the hiding "wrong" and not "a mistake"?
qa.a: She feels ashamed and wants Govind to hear her take full responsibility, not soften it; she is determined not to excuse herself.

qa.q: Which choice in Aparna's approach matters most for rebuilding, and why?
qa.a: Telling everything at once, with the paper of amounts and dates, matters most, because trust cannot start healing if new facts keep surfacing later.

qa.q: How might Govind feel when he hears about the earrings?
qa.a: He is likely hurt again and shaken, since it is a new secret, but also possibly relieved that it comes from her now rather than being discovered later.

grounding: Aparna gives Govind a complete account of her hidden loans at once and plainly calls the hiding wrong, showing that a single full disclosure matters more than a perfect one.

Aiko asked Wei to sit on the bench outside their apartment block in Osaka, where the children couldn't hear.

She had written it all in a notebook the night before, because she knew that if she spoke from memory she would leave things out to save face.

"The loan to Kenji was not one loan. It was three," she read. "The first in spring, the second in August. The third was last month, after you had already asked me whether there was anything else. I said no. That was a lie on top of the first lie."

Wei's shoulders dropped. He looked at the vending machine across the road, not at her.

"I'm not reading this so you'll forgive me today," Aiko said. "I'm reading it so that there's nothing left for you to find. If I've got a number slightly wrong, the notebook is yours. Check anything."

She closed it and handed it to him.

qa.q: What is Wei experiencing as he looks at the vending machine instead of at Aiko?

grounding: Aiko discloses every hidden loan to her brother in one written account and admits her earlier lie, showing full disclosure and accountability without waiting to be asked twice.

The family counselling centre in Nagpur had one small room with a ceiling fan that clicked on every turn. Kalyani, the counsellor, let the silence go on after Sameer said, "I keep finding things."

Rekha took a breath. "Then I'll say all of it now, in front of someone, so it can't change later."

She went through it: the loan she took for her brother's shop, the gold she used as security, the time she deleted the bank's messages from the family phone, and the second amount her brother asked for in the summer, which she also paid.

"I didn't tell you about the summer one even when you found the first," she said. "That was wrong. Hiding any of it was wrong. I kept thinking the next piece would be the last one you had to hear."

After the harvest money came in, Pradeep and Pooja walked together to the post office savings counter in their kasba, the first time in eleven years of marriage they had gone there together.

At home that evening Pooja drew two columns in the back of a school notebook. "Everything that comes in, everything that goes out. Both of us write. Both of us can read it any time."

"For how long?" Pradeep asked.

"Until you don't need to read it every day. Then maybe once a month."

Then the harder part. Her brother would need help again; everyone knew it. They agreed that from now on any help to either family, his or hers, would be decided together at this table, never alone.

"Even for your sister?" Pooja asked, half teasing.

Pradeep smiled for the first time that week. "Even for my sister."

He picked up the pen and wrote the first line himself.

qa.a: Two columns, one for everything that comes in and one for everything that goes out.

qa.q: What makes this arrangement likely to help rather than feel like a punishment?
qa.a: Both write in the notebook and both can read it, the family-help rule applies to both families, and they agree the daily checking will ease over time.

qa.q: How might this routine feel for Pooja?
qa.a: It gives her a way to prove she has changed, and she is likely hopeful and relieved that it is shared and temporary rather than one-sided watching.

On Sunday mornings in their Toronto apartment, Xin made coffee and Yosef opened the laptop, and for twenty minutes they looked at the shared budget together.

It had been Xin's idea, two months after he found out about the money she had sent her brother in Chengdu. "You can see everything, any time. Not in secret at night. With me."

"Every two weeks, then," Xin said. "Until we both say stop."

He looked at her. "You'd keep doing it even if I didn't ask?"

"It's not only for you," she said. "It helps me stop being the person who hides things."

They had come to add Siddharth's number to the alerts on Rajni's salary account, so he would get the same messages she did. It was Rajni's suggestion. After the loan she had hidden for her brother, she wanted him to stop guessing.

passage:
Dear Jeevan,

Since you asked what I honestly think after staying with you both last week, here it is.

On Tuesday you and Nisha were cooking together, laughing about the burnt rotis, and I thought: they're through it. On Thursday she got a call from her brother, stepped onto the balcony to take it, and I watched your whole face close. You barely spoke through dinner.

I don't think Thursday cancels Tuesday. From outside it looks like trust coming back in fits, a good week and then a bad evening when the memory flares. That seems normal to me, even if it's exhausting from inside.

But you also told me you still wake up angry some nights, a year on. If that doesn't ease, please think about seeing a counsellor together. Not to dig it all up again, but so you two can talk about it without it turning into the same fight.

I'm around. Call me when Thursdays happen.

Ritu

qa.q: What were Jeevan and Nisha laughing about on Tuesday?
qa.a: They were laughing about the burnt rotis while cooking together.

qa.q: What does Ritu seem to feel after watching Thursday's dinner?
qa.a: Ritu feels concerned for Jeevan but also hopeful, believing the bad evening does not cancel the good week.

qa.q: What does Ritu suggest if Jeevan's anger does not ease, and why is it a wise step?
qa.a: Ritu suggests seeing a counsellor together, because a counsellor could help them talk about it without it becoming the same fight again.

qa.q: What is it like for Jeevan when Nisha steps onto the balcony to take her brother's call?
qa.a: The memory flares; Jeevan may feel suspicious and hurt all over again, and Jeevan's face closes, with barely a word spoken through dinner.

grounding: Ritu, a friend, notices that trust between Jeevan and Nisha returns in fits and gently suggests a counsellor if Jeevan's hurt does not ease.

You asked what it looks like when a couple gets through something like that. I'm Kiran, and I've watched Mahima and Dev closely for about a year now, so I'll tell you what I saw.

It isn't a straight line. There was a stretch in spring where they came to every dinner holding hands, finishing each other's jokes, and I honestly thought, done, healed. Then one evening Mahima's brother turned up at our place unannounced, and I watched Dev go completely still. He left early. She sat in my kitchen afterwards saying, "I thought we were past this."

They weren't, not that night. But two weeks later they were fine again.

What helped, I think, was that neither of them treated the bad days as proof it had all failed. And when the bad days kept coming back around the same things, they started seeing a counsellor. Mahima says it lets them talk without scraping the wound open again. That's what I've seen, anyway.

qa.a: Mahima's brother.

passage:
Binita sits two desks from me at the insurance office, so I've had a front-row seat to the last few months, though I only know what she's chosen to tell me.

In January she barely ate lunch; she said things at home were "complicated" after her husband found out about a loan. By March she was showing me photos from a weekend trip they'd taken, all smiles. I thought it was over.

Then one Monday in April she came in with red eyes and said, "We had a bad day. He saw a message from my brother and it all came back."

I didn't know what to say, so I just said the good stretches probably still count.

Last week she mentioned they'd been to see a counsellor, because the bad days kept circling the same argument. She seemed lighter afterwards, or maybe I just wanted her to be.

— Avni

qa.q: What did Binita show Avni in March?
qa.a: Photos from a weekend trip they'd taken, all smiles.

qa.q: How does Avni feel watching Binita's ups and downs?
qa.a: Avni cares about Binita and feels hopeful, but is also unsure, admitting that Binita may only seem lighter because Avni wants her to be.

qa.q: Was Avni's reply on the red-eyed Monday helpful, and why?
qa.a: Yes; saying the good stretches still count was simple and kind, and it did not push Binita to explain more than she chose to.

qa.q: What is it like for Binita when a message from her brother brings it all back?
qa.a: It likely feels discouraging and painful, as if the good weeks were suddenly erased, even though they were real.

grounding: Avni, a colleague, observes Binita's marriage healing unevenly after a hidden loan, with good weeks and bad days, and notes that a counsellor helped.

passage:
Tuesday

Ma'am moved everyone around today and I got put next to the new girl, Aditi. I was annoyed because now I can't sit with Gurpreet.

But at lunch she took out a pile of cricket cards with a rubber band round them! The same series I collect!! She had the wicketkeeper card I have been looking for since summer holidays. I have two of the left-arm spinner so I asked if she wanted to swap.

She said yes straight away. Then she showed me a card that had a thumb mark printed on it by mistake and we both laughed so much Ma'am looked at us.

Tomorrow she is bringing her whole box. I am bringing mine.

Maybe the new seat is not so bad. 🙂

— Baljeet

qa.q: Which card had Baljeet been looking for since the summer holidays?
qa.a: The wicketkeeper card.

qa.q: How did Baljeet's feelings about the new seat change during the day?
qa.a: Baljeet was annoyed at first about not sitting with Gurpreet, but became excited and happy after discovering Aditi collects the same cricket cards.

qa.q: What small thing helped this friendship begin?
qa.a: Sitting on the same bench and sharing a game they both liked, the cards, plus laughing together at the misprinted card.

qa.q: How might Aditi, as the new girl, feel about Baljeet asking to swap?
qa.a: She is probably relieved and pleased that someone wanted to share something with her on a new seat in a new class.

grounding: Baljeet's diary shows a friendship starting from sharing a bench and a love of cricket cards, more than from knowing each other deeply.

passage:
The school bus from Kheda village had only one empty seat that morning, next to Minakshi, so Nandini squeezed in with her bag on her knees.

Then the bus hit a pothole, and a bundle of cricket cards slid out of Minakshi's bag and scattered across the floor.

Nandini dived to help pick them up. "You collect these? I have forty-two at home!"

Minakshi looked surprised. "My brothers say girls don't collect cricket cards."

"My brothers say that too," Nandini said. "They're wrong."

Nandini gave Minakshi one of her spare cards straight away.

That afternoon, Minakshi kept the seat next to her free with her tiffin box until Nandini climbed on. 😊

qa.q: How many cricket cards does Nandini have at home?
qa.a: Forty-two.

qa.q: Why does Minakshi keep the seat next to her free in the afternoon?
qa.a: She feels happy and wants to sit with Nandini again, hopeful that the shared interest on the bus can become a friendship.

qa.q: What did Nandini do on the bus that helped the friendship start?
qa.a: She helped pick up the scattered cards, shared her own interest, and gave Minakshi a spare card straight away.

qa.q: What was it like for Minakshi to hear "They're wrong" about girls collecting cards?
qa.a: It probably felt like relief and a small thrill, meeting someone who liked the same thing without laughing at her.

grounding: Nandini and Minakshi become friends because they share a bus seat and cricket cards, showing friendship at this age growing from proximity and shared interests.

passage:
On the first day of Year 4 in Leeds, Mrs Holt put Felix and Nour at the same table by the window because they were both new.

At break, Felix got out a small tin and began sorting his cricket cards on the table. Nour leaned over. "Is that a batting card or a bowling one?"

"Batting. You know cricket?"

"My dad watches it. I have three at home."

Felix pushed a spare card across the table. "You can have this one. I've got two."

Nour turned it over and read the funny line on the back about the player's favourite snack. They both laughed.

After lunch, she brought a scrap of paper and wrote CARD CLUB — TABLE 6 on it and stuck it on their table with her glue stick. Felix didn't take it down.

qa.q: What did Nour write on the scrap of paper after lunch?
qa.a: CARD CLUB — TABLE 6.

qa.q: What does Felix leaving the sign up suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he is pleased and happy to be part of something with Nour, even though he is shy and quiet.

qa.q: How could Mrs Holt support the two new children's friendship?
qa.a: She could keep them at the same table for a while and let them share the cards at break, since sitting together and sharing a game is how their friendship is growing.

qa.q: Why might Nour react to the spare card with a laugh rather than shyness?
qa.a: The funny line about the player's favourite snack gives them a shared joke, and she feels welcomed and relaxed.

grounding: Two new children seated together in Leeds start a friendship over cricket cards and a joke, showing friendship growing from a shared table and game.

passage:
Jagdish told Tarun his secret sitting on the wall behind the panchayat office after school.

"I still can't swim," he said, very fast. "Everyone thinks I can. I just stay near the steps at the pond."

Then he watched Tarun's face, ready to leave if Tarun laughed.

Tarun didn't laugh. He thought for a moment, then pulled half a guava out of his pocket and handed it over. "I can't ride a cycle without someone holding the back."

Jagdish grinned. "Really?"

"Don't tell Kishan."

"I won't."

The next week, when the boys went to the pond, Tarun stood near the steps too, and nobody asked why. Jagdish noticed. That evening he taught Tarun to pedal down the lane, holding the carrier the whole way, and then, just for a second, letting go.

qa.q: Where were Jagdish and Tarun sitting when Jagdish told his secret?
qa.a: On the wall behind the panchayat office after school.

qa.q: Why does Jagdish watch Tarun's face after telling him?
qa.a: He is nervous and wary, checking whether Tarun will laugh, because being laughed at would end the friendship.

qa.q: What small act showed Jagdish that Tarun could be trusted?
qa.a: Tarun did not laugh, shared his own secret, and later stood near the steps at the pond so Jagdish was not alone, keeping him safe.

qa.q: How does Tarun likely feel when Jagdish lets go of the cycle carrier for a second?
qa.a: He probably feels nervous but also trusting and excited, because Jagdish has now kept his secret safe too.

grounding: Jagdish and Tarun test each other's safety by trading small secrets and watching the reaction; being kept safe invites more trust.

passage:
Elif's grandmother packed her simit, sesame rings the other children in her Berlin class had called weird.

On Wednesday, Elif sat on the playground bench next to Liam and, without saying anything, broke one in half and held it out.

Liam looked at it. Elif held her breath.

He took it, bit into it, and said, "It's like a pretzel, but better."

Elif let her breath out. The next day she brought a whole one for him.

On Friday Liam returned the favour. He took out a small, squashed piece of honey cake. "My mum made it. It's a bit flat. Don't laugh."

Elif didn't laugh. She ate the whole thing and said it tasted like birthday.

Liam smiled and said nothing, but on Monday he saved her a place in the line for the climbing frame.

qa.q: What did the other children call Elif's simit in the first week?
qa.a: They called it weird.

qa.q: Why does Elif hold her breath when she offers Liam the simit?
qa.a: She is nervous and afraid he might call it weird or laugh, as the others had, which would end things.

qa.q: How did each child test the other, and what made it work?
qa.a: Each shared something a little risky, the simit and the flat honey cake, and watched for laughter; because neither laughed, they felt safe enough to share more.

qa.q: What might Liam have been feeling when he said "Don't laugh"?
qa.a: He was probably worried and a bit embarrassed about the squashed cake, testing whether Elif would keep him safe the way he had kept her safe.

grounding: Elif and Liam share snacks and watch each other's reactions; each kind response invites more trust, showing friendship testing safety.

passage:
The school library in Nashik had a rule of silence, so Madhuri wrote on a scrap of paper and slid it across to Sahil.

I am scared of the new maths sir.

She watched him read it. Her ears went hot. If he showed it to the boys at the back, she would never hear the end of it.

Sahil read it twice, then wrote underneath: Me too. He shouts. And folded it and pushed it back.

Madhuri almost laughed out loud. The next day during the maths period, when sir called on Madhuri and she froze, Sahil coughed loudly, which gave her a second to find the answer. Afterwards she found a new note in her pencil box: You were fine.

She kept that note inside the cover of her maths notebook for the rest of the year.

qa.q: What did Madhuri write on the first scrap of paper?
qa.a: I am scared of the new maths sir.

qa.q: What does Madhuri's hot ears tell us about how she feels after sliding the note over?
qa.a: She feels embarrassed and anxious, afraid Sahil might show it to the boys at the back and she would be teased.

qa.q: What went right in how Sahil responded to her secret?
qa.a: He kept it safe, shared that he felt the same, and later helped her quietly in class, which showed her she could trust him more.

qa.q: How might Sahil feel when Madhuri almost laughs at his note?
qa.a: He is probably relieved and pleased that his honest answer landed well and that she was not laughing at him.

grounding: Madhuri shares a small secret with Sahil and watches his reaction; because he keeps it safe and supports her, trust grows.

passage:
Nadia and Camila had walked home together in Valencia every day since October, the long way past the bakery.

They had a code now. Two taps on the desk meant "meet me at the fountain at break". Three taps meant "this lesson is SO boring". They had signed a paper in purple pen: BEST FRIENDS, NO ONE ELSE.

So when Nadia came out at break on Thursday and saw Camila playing hopscotch with Lucía and two other girls, her stomach dropped.

Camila waved. "Nadia! Come, we need one more!"

Nadia stood by the fountain, arms folded, and tapped twice on the stone rim.

At the bakery on the way home she finally said, "You said no one else."

Camila looked confused. "It was just hopscotch."

"It wasn't just hopscotch to me."

qa.q: What did two taps on the desk mean in Nadia and Camila's code?
qa.a: Two taps meant "meet me at the fountain at break".

qa.q: Why does Nadia's stomach drop when she sees Camila playing hopscotch?
qa.a: She feels hurt and a little jealous, because to her best friends meant no one else, and seeing Camila with other girls feels like being left out.

qa.q: What could Nadia try the next time she feels this way?
qa.a: She could join the game when invited, then tell Camila calmly later that she felt left out, instead of standing apart with her arms folded.

qa.q: How does Camila see the hopscotch game?
qa.a: To Camila it was just hopscotch and she even invited Nadia, so she is confused about why Nadia is upset.

grounding: Nadia and Camila's walks, secret codes and "best friends" promise show the joy of a close friendship, along with possessiveness and the first hurt at recess.

passage:
At the Dehradun hostel school, Alka and Wasim sat side by side in evening study hall and walked back together to the junior block every night.

They had invented a code: a pencil left pointing up on the desk meant "wait for me", pointing sideways meant "go ahead". "Best friends means forever," he'd said. "That's the rule."

On Saturday, during free play, Alka joined the badminton game with the girls from her dormitory. She forgot to look for Wasim.

At dinner he sat at the far end of the table, not looking at her.

"Nothing. Go play with your badminton friends."

Alka felt her face go hot. "I can have other friends and still be your best friend."

Wasim stabbed a potato. "It doesn't feel like it."

qa.q: What did a pencil pointing up on the desk mean?
qa.a: It meant "wait for me".

qa.q: What is Wasim feeling when he sits at the far end of the table and doesn't look at Alka?
qa.a: He feels hurt and left out, even a bit jealous, because to him best friends means forever and she played with others.

qa.q: How could a hostel warden or teacher support Alka and Wasim?
qa.a: They could help both say how they feel, and suggest ways Wasim could join some of the games so being best friends doesn't mean only each other.

qa.q: What is it like for Alka when Wasim says "Go play with your badminton friends"?
qa.a: She feels embarrassed and a bit unfairly blamed, since she did not mean to hurt him and believes she can have other friends too.

grounding: In a hostel, Alka and Wasim share walks, a code and a best-friends rule, and Wasim feels his first hurt when she plays with others at free time.

passage:
Monday. Hansa and Yamini walked home from school together for the first time, because Yamini's family had moved to the lane behind Hansa's. At the corner Yamini said, "You're my best friend now, okay?" Hansa said okay so fast she nearly tripped.

Wednesday, a week later. They had a secret code: pulling your left earlobe meant "look at who just walked in". They laughed so hard in assembly that Hansa got sent to the back. She didn't care.

Friday of the next week. At recess Yamini ran off to skip rope with Rupal and Mansi. Hansa waited on the steps with two halves of a mango she had saved. Yamini didn't come.

On the walk home Hansa didn't pull her earlobe once.

"Are you angry?" Yamini asked.

Hansa shrugged. "You said best friends."

"You are my best friend. I just like skipping."

qa.q: What did pulling your left earlobe mean in their code?
qa.a: It meant "look at who just walked in".

qa.q: How can you tell Hansa feels hurt on the walk home?
qa.a: She doesn't pull her earlobe once, shrugs, and says "You said best friends"; she feels hurt and possessive after waiting alone with the mango.

qa.q: What could Hansa try next time Yamini plays with other girls at recess?
qa.a: She could ask to join the skipping or tell Yamini she saved her mango, instead of waiting alone and saying nothing until later.

qa.q: How does Yamini see the recess skipping?
qa.a: Yamini sees no conflict: Hansa is still her best friend and she just likes skipping, so she is a little puzzled that Hansa is angry.

grounding: Across three days Hansa and Yamini walk home, invent a code and call each other best friends, then Hansa feels her first hurt when Yamini plays with others at recess.

passage:
In the first week of term, Mahima Ma'am watched Naveen and Irfan share one tin of crayons in the art room, heads almost touching.

Three weeks later, on the Monday after the football trials, Naveen came to art in muddy socks and sat with the football boys. Irfan kept an empty stool beside him until the bell, then moved his bag onto it.

By the end of the month, Mahima Ma'am noticed they no longer waited for each other at the gate. Naveen ran to the field; Irfan stayed back to finish the class mural with the art club. Neither seemed angry; they still waved across the corridor.

She thought about seating them together, then decided not to. Instead she asked Irfan to lead the mural group, and asked Naveen to paint the football match in one corner of it.

qa.q: Where did Naveen and Irfan sit together in the first week of term?
qa.a: In the art room, sharing one tin of crayons.

qa.q: What does Mahima Ma'am seem to think when she decides not to move the boys together?
qa.a: She seems to understand that neither boy did anything wrong and feels it would be unfair to force them back; she is thoughtful and a little wistful as they drift apart.

qa.q: What was wise about the way Mahima Ma'am included both boys in the mural?
qa.a: She let each keep his new interest, Irfan leading the art group and Naveen painting football, while still giving them one shared project.

qa.q: How might Irfan feel when he moves his bag onto the empty stool?
qa.a: He probably feels disappointed and a little lonely, realising Naveen is now spending time with the football boys.

grounding: A teacher, Mahima Ma'am, notices over a month how football and art pull two friends into different groups without either doing anything wrong.

passage:
Baljeet, you're upset because Sunny has started playing chess with those other boys. When I taught in Ludhiana, long ago, I saw something like it.

I had two girls in my class, Pammi and Nimmo. Inseparable. Same tiffin, same plaits, same everything. Then Pammi joined the kabaddi team. Nimmo stayed with the girls who embroidered in the lunch break.

I was worried. I thought one of them must have hurt the other. So I kept Nimmo back one afternoon and asked her gently. She looked at me, puzzled. "Nothing happened, Tanuja Ma'am. Pammi just likes kabaddi now."

That was when I understood. Nobody had done anything wrong. They had simply started liking different things, and different things come with different people.

They stayed friendly. At the school fair, Pammi bought one of Nimmo's embroidered handkerchiefs.

qa.q: Which team did Pammi join?
qa.a: The kabaddi team.

qa.q: What was Tanuja worried about before talking to Nimmo?
qa.a: Tanuja was worried and concerned that one girl must have hurt the other, since they had been inseparable.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Tanuja saw the two girls?
qa.a: Keeping Nimmo back and gently asking her; Nimmo's puzzled answer that nothing happened helped Tanuja see no one had done anything wrong.

qa.q: How did Nimmo seem to feel about Pammi joining kabaddi?
qa.a: Nimmo seemed calm and a little puzzled by the question, accepting that Pammi just liked kabaddi now, and she stayed friendly with her.

grounding: Tanuja, a former teacher, recalls noticing two close friends drift into kabaddi and embroidery groups without anyone doing wrong.

passage:
It had rained for three days, so Usha Ma'am ran the Class 5 PT period inside the school hall in Guwahati: football on one side, the drawing club on the other.

Until last month, Ganga had never been without Jyoti. Now Ganga was in goal, shouting and laughing with her new team. Jyoti sat at the other end with the drawing club, sketching the rain on the windows.

At the water break, Ganga ran past Jyoti's corner. Usha Ma'am saw her slow down, as if she might stop, and then keep going when someone called her name from the goal.

Jyoti looked up, then back at her sketch.

Usha Ma'am wondered whether to say something. There had been no quarrel, nothing to fix. She decided to ask Jyoti if she would draw the football team for the class noticeboard. Jyoti smiled and turned to a new page.

qa.q: Why was PT held inside the school hall?
qa.a: It had rained for three days.

qa.q: What was Usha Ma'am feeling as she wondered whether to say something?
qa.a: She was unsure and a little concerned for Jyoti, but she recognised there had been no quarrel and nothing to fix.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Asking Jyoti to draw the football team worked, because it respected her art interest and gently linked her to Ganga's new group without forcing anything.

qa.q: What is it like for Ganga when she slows down near Jyoti's corner and then keeps going?
qa.a: She may feel torn and a little guilty, caught between her old friend and her new team who are calling her name.

grounding: Usha Ma'am, a teacher, notices on a rainy day how Ganga's football and Jyoti's drawing have pulled them into different groups without any fault.
